title: Amazon E-Commerce: Complete Architecture
description: Design an Amazon-scale global e-commerce platform with distributed inventory, shopping cart, SAGA checkout orchestration, and search.

data.text: Design a global e-commerce platform at Amazon scale. The system serves 300+ million active customers browsing a catalog of over 350 million products across thousands of categories. During peak flash sales and events like Prime Day, the platform handles over 100,000 order placements per second. Core engineering challenges include zero overselling of scarce inventory, sub-100ms catalog search and browsing, fault-tolerant multi-step checkout via distributed transactions, and decoupled fulfillment logistics.

terms.definition: A coordinator that executes a series of local transactions across microservices, executing compensating actions if any step fails.
Reserving stock with an expiration TTL during checkout (Soft Hold) and finalizing deduction upon successful payment (Hard Commit).
Separating read and write models: writes hit transactional DBs; reads query optimized Elasticsearch clusters and Redis caches.
A unique client-supplied token (UUID) ensuring duplicate payment or order submission requests execute exactly once.
Locking mechanisms across Redis nodes ensuring only one process modifies a high-demand SKU stock counter simultaneously.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Product Catalog: Browse, filter by attributes, and full-text search across 350M+ items with facet counts
Shopping Cart: Fast add/update/remove items, sync across guest and logged-in states, persist for 30+ days
Inventory Management: Real-time stock visibility, reservation lock during checkout, stock decrement on payment
Order & Checkout: Multi-step checkout (address, shipping speed, payment), discount vouchers, order tracking
Payment Processing: Integration with card networks, wallets, gift cards, and third-party payment gateways with retry mechanisms
Personalized Recommendations: "Customers who bought this also bought...", recently viewed items
Post-Order Fulfillment: Warehouse dispatching, tracking updates, invoice generation, and refunds

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Traffic: 100,000 orders/second peak (Prime Day); 500,000 search queries/second
Latency: <100ms P99 for catalog search & product detail pages; <1.5s for checkout completion
Data Consistency: Strict consistency for inventory and payments (zero double-deductions); eventual consistency for reviews and recommendations
Availability: 99.999% for product browsing and cart; 99.99% for order placement
Durability: Zero lost orders once payment is authorized (write-ahead event logs)
Security: PCI-DSS compliance for payment card processing, end-to-end data encryption

data.text: The architecture decouples high-throughput read operations (Catalog, Search, Product Display) from transactional write operations (Cart, Order, Payment, Inventory). An event-driven backbone powered by Kafka ensures asynchronous downstream processing for shipping, notifications, and analytics.

data.text: Order Placement: SAGA Distributed Transaction Flow

To maintain high availability without holding distributed two-phase commit (2PC) locks across independent databases, checkout uses an Orchestrated SAGA pattern. If payment authorization fails or inventory runs out, compensating transactions rollback previous reservations.

data.caption: SAGA Orchestration sequence for order placement with inventory lock and compensating rollback upon payment failure
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Customer as 👤 Customer
    participant GW as 🚪 API Gateway
    participant Orch as ⚡ SAGA Orchestrator
    participant Inv as 🏷️ Inventory
    participant Pay as 💳 Payment
    participant Order as 📋 Order DB
    participant Kafka as 📨 Kafka

    Customer->>GW: POST /checkout
    GW->>Orch: Start SAGA
    Orch->>Order: Create Order (PENDING)
    Order-->>Orch: OrderCreated

    Orch->>Inv: ReserveStock
    alt Stock Available
        Inv-->>Orch: StockReserved
    else Stock Insufficient
        Inv-->>Orch: Failed
        Orch->>Order: Cancel (OUT_OF_STOCK)
        Orch-->>GW: 409 Error
        GW-->>Customer: Out of stock
    end

    Orch->>Pay: AuthorizePayment
    alt Payment Success
        Pay-->>Orch: Authorized
        Orch->>Inv: CommitStock
        Inv-->>Orch: Committed
        Orch->>Order: Confirm Order
        Orch->>Kafka: Publish OrderConfirmed
        Orch-->>GW: 201 Created
        GW-->>Customer: Order confirmed
    else Payment Failed
        Pay-->>Orch: Failed
        Note over Orch, Inv: Compensating Transaction
        Orch->>Inv: ReleaseStock
        Inv-->>Orch: Released
        Orch->>Order: Mark Failed
        Orch-->>GW: 402 Error
        GW-->>Customer: Payment failed
    end

faqs.question: How to prevent overselling when 50,000 users buy the same limited item simultaneously?
faqs.answer: Store real-time available stock in Redis using an atomic Lua script that checks and decrements the balance: `if redis.call("get", KEYS[1]) >= ARGV[1] then return redis.call("decrby", KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) else return -1 end`. Only users who receive a non-negative response advance to checkout. Failed requests fail instantly in <5ms without touching relational databases.

faqs.question: Why use an Orchestrated SAGA instead of 2-Phase Commit (2PC)?
faqs.answer: 2PC requires holding locks across multiple microservice databases (Inventory, Order, Payment) until the entire transaction concludes. If any network partition or service latency occurs, locks hang and cascade into system-wide failure. SAGA replaces distributed locks with local ACID transactions coupled with asynchronous compensating rollbacks, ensuring resilience and horizontal scale.

faqs.question: How is the shopping cart designed for cross-device consistency and high availability?
faqs.answer: Use Amazon DynamoDB partitioned by `UserID`. For anonymous users, the cart is tied to a session cookie. When the user logs in, a Cart Merge Service reconciles guest items with their persistent user cart. DynamoDB provides single-digit millisecond latency and scales automatically with zero maintenance.

faqs.question: How is catalog search kept fast and fresh with 350M items and frequent price updates?
faqs.answer: Search uses Elasticsearch clusters separated from write databases. Price and stock availability change constantly and bypass search indexing; they are queried in real time from a distributed Redis cache layer when rendering product listings, avoiding the indexing overhead of millions of Elasticsearch document updates per second.

faqs.question: How does the platform handle idempotent payments?
faqs.answer: Every checkout request generates a unique client-side `Idempotency-Key` (UUIDv4) stored in Redis with a 24-hour TTL alongside transaction state. If a user double-clicks "Place Order" or a network timeout prompts an automatic retry, the payment gateway detects the active or completed key and returns the original response without double-charging.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CQRS separates catalog reads (Elasticsearch + Redis) from transactional writes (PostgreSQL + DynamoDB)
SAGA Orchestration coordinates checkout across Order, Inventory, and Payment services with automatic compensation
Two-phase inventory reservation with Redis atomic Lua scripts protects against overselling during flash sales
Idempotency keys on checkout prevent duplicate payments from network retries or user double-submissions
Event-driven Kafka architecture handles downstream shipping, notifications, and analytics asynchronously
data.takeaway: Amazon-scale e-commerce relies on decoupling high-frequency browsing from strict ACID transactions. Fast in-memory atomic locks guard stock allocation while SAGA state machines ensure resilient, fault-tolerant checkout workflows.
